## Synthesis: research report

**Question:** Research the state of the art in web visual design vocabulary, to extend the reference library of an agent-run pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me). The pipeline already documents 32 named visual styles across 7 families (surface/material, structural, atmospheric, motion-native, technical/data, textural, reductive) and 72 rendering techniques across 6 groups (GPU/rendering, post-processing, CSS+SVG native, motion/input, whole-page, typographic craft). Its documented GAP is everything about PRESENTING INFORMATION — it has no data-visualization vocabulary and no component-pattern vocabulary at all.

COVER ALL SIX AREAS:

1. DATA AND INFORMATION VISUALIZATION — chart type selection and when each is the right encoding; perceptual ranking of visual encodings (position/length/angle/area/color) and the research behind it; sequential, diverging and categorical color scale construction (including OKLCH/perceptually-uniform approaches and colorblind-safe palettes); small multiples; sparklines and in-line micro-charts; dashboard and stat-tile layout patterns; data storytelling and scrollytelling (scroll-linked chart transitions, annotation layers); editorial data-graphics conventions from newsrooms (NYT, FT, Pudding, Reuters); table design at density (tabular numerals, decimal alignment, hairline rules, sticky headers); how to present evidence and provenance so figures are checkable; accessible charts (screen-reader alternatives, non-color encoding, focus order).

2. COMPONENT AND CONTAINER PATTERNS — cards and their many failure modes; documented ALTERNATIVES to the card grid for presenting a body of projects or work (editorial indexes, tables-as-index, list-with-hover-preview, timelines, maps, filmstrips, stacked/scroll-driven layouts, masonry critiques, single-item-at-a-time patterns, hub-and-spoke); drawers, sheets, side panels, bottom sheets and their platform conventions; modals versus inline expansion versus routed pages, and when each is correct; progressive disclosure patterns; accordions and details/summary; lists — dense, editorial, and interactive; empty, loading and error states as designed deliverables; navigation patterns beyond a top bar.

3. NEW AND EMERGING VISUAL STYLE MOVEMENTS — named aesthetic movements in web and interface design current as of 2025-2026 that are NOT in the list above; include their defining mechanics, their characteristic failure mode, and the condition under which they are the right choice. Also cover which looks now read as generic, templated, or AI-default (so they can be avoided), and the discourse on distinctive versus homogenized web design.

4. MOTION AND INTERACTION FOR THE ABOVE — how cards, drawers, lists and charts should actually behave; shared-element and container transforms; the View Transitions API; disclosure and expansion motion; chart entrance, transition and morphing animation; staggering and orchestration; scroll-linked and scroll-driven reveals; spring/physics versus duration-and-easing, and when each is right.

5. MICRO-INTERACTIONS AND MICRO-ANIMATION — the anatomy and principles of a micro-interaction; feedback, state change and affordance signalling; hover, focus, press and drag states; optimistic UI; haptics; sound; the timing, easing and duration ranges that read as responsive versus sluggish, with the research or platform guidance behind the numbers.

6. LOADING, PROGRESS AND PERCEIVED PERFORMANCE — skeleton screens versus spinners versus progress indicators and the evidence for each; designed preloaders; streaming and progressive rendering; optimistic and predictive loading; perceived-performance research including documented duration thresholds; layout-shift avoidance.

CONSTRAINTS THAT MAKE A FINDING USABLE — prefer and clearly flag findings that satisfy these, and flag ones that violate them:
- Web-native and implementable in HTML/CSS/SVG/canvas/WebGL. Note when a pattern is CSS/SVG-native (cheap) versus requiring a heavy runtime.
- Two-tier budget: a shell under 100KB (HTML, critical CSS, subset fonts, minimal JS) that paints alone with LCP under 1.5s, and a deferred heavy layer. Note byte cost and whether a technique can be deferred.
- Every technique must ship three states: full, a DESIGNED reduced-motion still (never `animation: none`), and a no-WebGL/no-canvas fallback.
- Accessibility is non-negotiable: WCAG contrast, keyboard operability, focus management (especially for drawers, sheets and modals — focus trap, restore, escape, inert background), screen-reader semantics, and non-color encodings.
- Self-hosted and vendored: no CDN in production, no third-party badge or chart services, no hotlinked stock imagery. Visuals are generated (CSS, SVG, canvas, WebGL, procedural) or generated-then-treated in-browser.
- Anti-template: the pipeline's core rule is that two runs must never look alike, so favour findings that support distinctiveness and explicitly name what has become a cliché.

DELIVERABLE — a survey report first: the landscape per area, with concrete named patterns, the mechanics of each, its documented failure mode, the condition under which it is right, and citations. Prefer primary and authoritative sources: peer-reviewed HCI and visualization research, Nielsen Norman Group, MDN and W3C/WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, platform human-interface guidelines (Apple HIG, Material Design), the published work of newsroom graphics desks, and named practitioners — over listicles and SEO content. Where a number is claimed (a duration threshold, a byte weight, a perceptual ranking), attribute it to its source and note if it is folklore rather than measured. THEN, in a clearly separated final section, map the findings to the repo: which belong as new STYLES.md entries (four-part shape: mechanics / Implies / Fails / Right when), which as new or extended CRAFT.md technique groups (table shape: Technique / What it is / Where it earns its place), and which are new material entirely — flagging any that conflict with the existing rules.

14 claims survived 3-vote adversarial verification. Merge semantic duplicates and synthesize.

## Confirmed claims
### [0] Cleveland & McGill establish the canonical perceptual ranking of visual encodings as six accuracy tiers, most-to-least accurate: (1) position along a common scale, (2) position along nonaligned scales, (3) length/direction/angle, (4) area, (5) volume/curvature, (6) shading/color saturation. Ties within tiers 3, 5 and 6 are explicitly unresolved — the paper states there was not enough information to separate them. The accompanying design rule is to encode using the highest tier available. Note this ranking is HYPOTHESIZED from psychophysics plus prior work, and only tiers 1 vs 2 vs 3 were experimentally tested in this paper; area, volume and color rankings are theoretical here, not measured.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: http://faculty.washington.edu/aragon/classes/hcde511/s12/readings/cleveland84.pdf (primary)
Quote: "The following are the 10 elementary tasks in Figure 1, ordered from most to least accurate: 1. Position along a common scale 2. Positions along nonaligned scales 3. Length, direction, angle 4. Area 5. Volume, curvature 6. Shading, color saturation ... Three of the ranks—3, 5, and 6—have more than one task; at the moment there is not enough information to separate the ties. ... The theory provides a guideline for graph construction: Graphs should employ elementary tasks as high in the ordering as possible."
Verifier evidence (high): I extracted full text from the JSTOR scan of the primary paper (Cleveland & McGill 1984, JASA 79(387):531-554) and verified every load-bearing element verbatim. Extracted text at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-taha/b7953e86-7295-434f-af62-abc041f9f51e/scratchpad/webfetch-1785152133788-ud1wvx.pdf.txt.

CONFIRMED VERBATIM:
1. The six-tier list, exactly as claimed (p.535-536): "The following are the 10 elementary tasks in Figure 1, ordered from most to least accurate: 1. Position along a common scale 2. Positions along nonaligned scales 3. Length, direction, angle 4. Area 5. Volume, curvature 6. Shading, color saturation".
2. The ties sentence (p.537): "Three of the ranks-3, 5, and 6-have more than one task; at the moment there is not enough information to separate the ties."
3. The design rule, verbatim in the abstract: "The theory provides a guideline for graph construction: Graphs should employ elementary tasks as high in the ordering as possible."
4. "HYPOTHESIZED" is the paper's own word, not the claimant's gloss (p.535): "In this section we hypothesize an ordering of the 10 elementary perceptual tasks on the basis of the accuracy with which people can extract quantitative information by using them." And on basis (p.537): "The hypothesized ordering of the elementary tasks is based on information from a variety of sources: our own reasoning and experimentation with various graph forms, results of psychophysical experiments, and the theory of psychophysics."
5. Area/volume are explicitly theoretical, not measured here (p.537-538): "length judgments are hypothesized to be more accurate than area judgments, which in turn are hypothesized to be more accurate than volume judgments. This ordering is based on a combination of psychophysical theory and experimental results" — i.e. imported prior results, no experiment in this paper.

ONE CORRECTION REQUIRED (does not overturn the claim; it errs in the paper's favour, over-crediting the experiments). The claim says "only tiers 1 vs 2 vs 3 were experimentally tested." Tier 2 was NOT tested. Section 4.2 states the position-length experiment used only "Judgment Types 1-3, subjects had to judge position along a common scale, and for Judgment Types 4 and 5, subjects had to judge length"; the second was the position-angle (bar vs pie) experiment. Section 4.1 summarises: "The experiments demonstrated very clearly that some judgments of position along a common scale are more accurate than some judgments of length and of angle." Tier 2's rank rests solely on a Weber's-Law argument about framed rectangles ("The reason for putting position along nonaligned scales ahead of length is that there are additional visual cues"). Correct wording: only tier 1 vs tier 3 (length, and separately angle) was experimentally tested; tiers 2, 4, 5, 6 are theoretical in this paper.

TWO QUALIFICATIONS TO CARRY INTO THE REPORT (neither refutes the claim): (a) the paper itself limits the rule's force — "The ordering of the perceptual tasks does not provide a complete prescription for how to make a graph. Rather, it provides a set of guidelines that must be used with judgment in designing a graph"; and the authors concede overlap — "it might be argued that judging positions along nonaligned scales really involves making two length judgments". (b) Downstream literature qualifies the ranking's generality: Heer & Bostock (CHI 2010) replicated position>length>angle on Mechanical Turk and extended it to circular/rectangular area, while McColeman et al., "The Risks of Ranking" (arXiv:2212.10533), find the encoding rankings do not hold under a different task and that factors such as cardinality outweigh encoding choice. So the ranking should be cited as a design prior, not a law.

Source quality: primary, peer-reviewed JASA paper, cited directly; claim is historical so "outdated" does not apply; no marketing content involved.

### [1] The accuracy advantage of position over length and angle is MEASURED, not folklore: two controlled experiments (51 subjects with usable data each, judging bar charts and pie charts on 'what percentage is one value of a larger value') found position judgments more accurate than length judgments by factors of 1.4 to 2.5, and 1.96 times as accurate as angle judgments. These are the specific numbers to attribute when claiming position beats angle — i.e. bar chart beats pie chart by roughly a factor of 2.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: http://faculty.washington.edu/aragon/classes/hcde511/s12/readings/cleveland84.pdf (primary)
Quote: "In both experiments there were 51 subjects with usable data. ... In the first experiment, position judgments were more accurate than length judgments by factors varying from 1.4 to 2.5. In the second experiment, position judgments were 1.96 times as accurate as angle judgments."
Verifier evidence (high): VERIFIED VERBATIM AGAINST THE PRIMARY SOURCE. I downloaded the PDF (JSTOR scan of Cleveland & McGill, "Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods," JASA 79(387), Sept 1984, pp. 531–554) and read the image pages directly (pdftotext only yields the JSTOR cover; body pages are CCITT scans, so I read them visually).

The supporting quote is verbatim from Section 4.5 "Summary of the Experiments," p. 544: "Two experiments were run in which subjects judged bar charts and pie charts. In the first experiment, five types of judgments were made—two length judgments and three judgments of position along a common scale. In the second experiment, there were two types of judgment—position and angle. For all types of judgments, subjects made visual assessments of what percentage one value was of a larger value; thus all recorded values were between 0 and 100. In both experiments there were 51 subjects with usable data. ... In the first experiment, position judgments were more accurate than length judgments by factors varying from 1.4 to 2.5. In the second experiment, position judgments were 1.96 times as accurate as angle judgments."

Every component checks out independently elsewhere in the paper:
- Subject counts (§4.3, p. 539): position–length experiment ran 55 subjects, 4 deleted for not following instructions; position–angle ran 54, 3 deleted. "For both experiments, 51 subjects remained for analysis." So "51 with usable data each" is correct, not a single pooled 51.
- Chart types in Exp 2 (p. 539): "54 subjects judged the two types of graphs shown in Figure 3; one type was a pie chart and the other was an ordinary bar chart." So the gloss "bar chart beats pie chart by roughly a factor of 2" is a literal description of Experiment 2, not an extrapolation.
- Derivation of the numbers (p. 541): errors measured as log2(|judged% − true%| + 1/8), location estimated by midmean. Position–length: "The larger of the two length values is 1.32 log units greater than the smallest of the three position values, which is a factor of 2^1.32 = 2.5. The smaller length value is .51 log units greater than the largest position value, which is a factor of 1.4." Position–angle: "The difference is .97 on the log scale, which is a factor of 2^.97 = 1.96, and is statistically significant." Arithmetic confirmed (2^0.97 = 1.9585). 95% CIs via bootstrap (1,000 resamples of size 51), Figure 16.
- Corroborating detail (p. 540): "In only 3 of the 40 cases was the pie chart more accurate on average than the bar chart." Large-error rates (p. 542): angle judgments produced large errors at 7.3x the position rate; length at 5.3x.

SOURCE QUALITY: peer-reviewed JASA, the field's foundational primary experiment — matches or exceeds the claim's strength. Not marketing, not a listicle, not forum speculation.

CONTRADICTION SEARCH: no credible source disputes the numbers. Heer & Bostock, CHI 2010 "Crowdsourcing Graphical Perception" replicated the Cleveland–McGill position/length/angle/area stimuli on Mechanical Turk and obtained results very similar to the original. The genuine critiques (McColeman, Yang, Brady, Franconeri, "Rethinking the Ranks of Visual Channels," IEEE TVCG 2021, arXiv:2107.11367; also Simkin & Hastie 1987 JASA and Spence & Lewandowsky 1991) do not dispute the 1984 measurements — they challenge the GENERALIZABILITY of the derived ranking, arguing two-value ratio judgment is a narrow proxy for real chart tasks and that some individuals credibly deviate from the canonical ordering.

TWO CAVEATS TO CARRY FORWARD, neither refuting:
1. Scope. The numbers hold for one task — "what percentage one value was of a larger value" — on specific 1984 print stimuli. The authors themselves hedge on p. 538: "Strictly speaking we cannot do more than assert that the results hold for the particular types of graphs in the experiment." Do NOT let the survey report state a universal "bars beat pies" law; part-of-whole and summation tasks are the documented exception (Spence & Lewandowsky 1991).
2. "Accuracy" here is the ratio of midmean log2 absolute-error magnitudes, not a hit rate; and 1.4–2.5 are the BOUNDS across best/worst position–length pairings, not a single uniform effect. Exp 1 used grouped and divided bar charts only — no pie charts — so "judging bar charts and pie charts" is the paper's own collective phrasing across both experiments, not per-experiment.

Verdict: the claim's central assertion — that the position-over-length-and-angle advantage is measured rather than folklore, with these specific attributable figures — is fully supported by the primary source.

### [2] Gross failure, not just average error, is far more frequent for lower-tier encodings: large errors (log error > 4) occurred 5.3x more often for length judgments than position judgments (136 of 2,550 judgments), and 7.3x more often for angle judgments than position judgments (219 of 4,080 judgments). Encoding choice therefore governs catastrophic misreading rate, not merely precision — a stronger argument against pie/angle encodings than the mean-accuracy factor alone.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: http://faculty.washington.edu/aragon/classes/hcde511/s12/readings/cleveland84.pdf (primary)
Quote: "Of the 2,550 judgments made by the subjects, 136 had a log error greater than 4. ... Seventy-eight percent of the large errors occurred for the length judgments; since there were three position judgments for each two length judgments, the rate of occurrence of large errors for length judgments is 5.3 times that for position judgments. ... in this experiment 219 of the 4,080 judgments had large errors. Eighty-eight percent of the large errors occurred for the angle judgments; thus the rate of occurrence of large errors for the angle judgments is 7.3 times that for the position judgments."
Verifier evidence (high): I OCR-read the actual JSTOR scan of Cleveland & McGill 1984 (JASA 79(387):531–554) at the cited URL. The quote is VERBATIM from pp. 541–542, section headed "Large Absolute Errors" (accompanying Figure 17, "Percentage of large errors"):

p.541: "The top panel of Figure 17 shows a summary of the large errors for the position–length experiment. Of the 2,550 judgments made by the subjects, 136 had a log error greater than 4."
p.542: "Seventy-eight percent of the large errors occurred for the length judgments; since there were three position judgments for each two length judgments, the rate of occurrence of large errors for length judgments is 5.3 times that for position judgments. ... in this experiment 219 of the 4,080 judgments had large errors. Eighty-eight percent of the large errors occurred for the angle judgments; thus the rate of occurrence of large errors for the angle judgments is 7.3 times that for the position judgments."

ARITHMETIC CROSS-CHECK against the design described on pp.539–540 — all self-consistent, which rules out a garbled or hallucinated quote:
- 51 subjects retained after exclusions (p.539); position–length = 50 judgments/subject (10 ratios x 5 types) → 51x50 = 2,550. Position–angle = 80 judgments/subject (40 ratios x 2 types) → 51x80 = 4,080. Both totals match exactly.
- Types 1–3 = position along a common scale, Types 4–5 = length (p.539), i.e. 3 position : 2 length. Recomputing: 0.78x136 = 106 length errors / 1,020 length judgments = 10.4%; 0.22x136 = 30 / 1,530 = 1.96%; ratio = 5.32 ≈ 5.3. ✓
- Position–angle is 1:1 (2,040 each): 0.88x219 = 193/2,040 = 9.45%; 0.12x219 = 26/2,040 = 1.29%; ratio = 7.33 ≈ 7.3. ✓
- Threshold decoded: error = log2(|judged% − true%| + 1/8) (p.540), so "log error > 4" = absolute error > 15.9 percentage points on a 0–100 scale. Calling that "gross failure" is fair, not inflation.

THE INTERPRETIVE STEP HOLDS TOO. The claim's comparative ("stronger than the mean-accuracy factor alone") is arithmetically true against the paper's own mean figures: angle vs position mean difference is ".97 on the log scale, which is a factor of 2^.97 = 1.96" (p.541); length vs position "40%–250% larger" (1.4x–2.5x). 5.3x and 7.3x exceed both. Critically, the paper states it used MIDMEANS "principally because of the outliers" (p.540) — so the headline mean factors deliberately trim exactly these tails, which is why the large-error rate is genuinely additional information rather than a restatement. Angle stimuli were pie charts and position stimuli bar charts (p.539), so "pie/angle" is the authors' own framing, not the claimant's invention. Blunder confounds are ruled out: "Only four errors occurred in the choice of which bar or segment was smaller" (p.539).

CAVEATS TO CARRY INTO THE REPORT (qualify, do not refute): (1) The >4 threshold is post-hoc and unpreregistered; no test statistic or CI is reported for either ratio, and judgments are clustered within 51 subjects, so these are descriptive rates, not inferential — the word "governs" is stronger than the paper's own language. (2) The paper itself hedges generalization: "Strictly speaking we cannot do more than assert that the results hold for the particular types of graphs in the experiment" (p.538). (3) The "against pie/angle" gloss is contested downstream — Spence & Lewandowsky (Applied Cognitive Psychology 1991, 5(1):61–77) found "little to choose between the pie and bar chart," with pie better for combination judgments; Skau & Kosara (EuroVis/CGF 2016, 35(3):121–130) and Kosara (IEEE VIS Short 2019, "Evidence for Area as the Primary Visual Cue in Pie Charts") found angle is the LEAST used cue in pie reading, so the mechanism label "angle" is likely wrong even if pie decoding is worse. None of these dispute the 5.3x/7.3x numbers themselves. Recommend the report cite the statistic as scoped to Cleveland & McGill's bar-vs-pie stimuli and pair it with the Skau/Kosara mechanism correction.

SOURCE QUALITY: peer-reviewed JASA, the foundational primary paper, read directly rather than via secondary summary; main ranking independently replicated by Heer & Bostock (CHI 2010). Not marketing, not a listicle, not a benchmark. 1984 date is not disqualifying for a perceptual finding of this kind.

### [3] The paper's applied conclusion is that pie charts, divided bar charts, and shaded statistical maps (choropleths) are not fixable by refinement and should be REPLACED, and it names three specific replacement forms: dot charts, dot charts with grouping, and framed-rectangle charts. Choropleth shading is condemned because shading/color saturation sits in the LAST accuracy tier. Length and angle judgments also carry consistent bias: subjects systematically underestimate when true percentages fall in the 25-50 range.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: http://faculty.washington.edu/aragon/classes/hcde511/s12/readings/cleveland84.pdf (primary)
Quote: "The conclusion is that radical surgery on these popular graphs is needed, and as replacements we offer alternative graphical forms—dot charts, dot charts with grouping, and framed-rectangle charts. ... An important part of the contribution to the errors for length and angle judgments is consistent bias. When the true percentages are in the range of 25–50%, subjects tend to underestimate values for these types of judgments."
Verifier evidence (high): VERIFIED AGAINST PRIMARY SOURCE, NOT JUST THE SUPPLIED QUOTE. The linked faculty.washington.edu PDF is a scan with no text layer (pdftotext yields only the 1.4KB JSTOR cover page), so I pulled an identical-pagination JSTOR copy of Cleveland & McGill, JASA 79(387):531-554 (statsclass.com/dsci310/Notes/Cleveland_McGill_EPT.pdf) and grepped the full text. All four components check out verbatim:

(1) Abstract, verbatim: "This principle is applied to a variety of graphs, including bar charts, divided bar charts, pie charts, and statistical maps with shading. The conclusion is that radical surgery on these popular graphs is needed, and as replacements we offer alternative graphical forms-dot charts, dot charts with grouping, and framed-rectangle charts." Restated in the Introduction as "The disconcerting conclusion is that radical surgery on these popular types of graphs is needed..." So the "replace, not refine" framing and the exact three replacement forms are the authors' own words, not a paraphrase.

(2) The perceptual ordering is printed as a numbered list: "1. Position along a common scale / 2. Positions along nonaligned scales / 3. Length, direction, angle / 4. Area / 5. Volume, curvature / 6. Shading, color saturation." Shading/color saturation is indeed the last (6th) tier.

(3) The choropleth condemnation is a titled section: "5.3 Framed-Rectangle Charts as Replacements for Statistical Maps With Shading", opening "Statistical maps that use shading (or color saturation or color hue) to encode a real variable, which Tukey (1979) called patch maps..." — confirming both the target and the stated rationale.

(4) The bias sentence is verbatim: "An important part of the contribution to the errors for length and angle judgments is consistent bias. When the true percentages are in the range of 25-50, subjects tend to underestimate values for these types of judgments." (Same passage also reports position judgments 1.96x as accurate as angle judgments.)

ATTEMPTED REFUTATIONS THAT FAILED: (a) omission — the claim lists three targets but the paper names four ("bar charts, divided bar charts, pie charts, and statistical maps with shading"); this is incompleteness, not error, since the claim never says "only these". (b) Source strength — this is a primary peer-reviewed JASA article, adequate for a claim about its own contents.

QUALIFICATIONS THE PIPELINE MUST CARRY (they qualify, not refute): The 6-tier ordering is NOT a measured accuracy ranking. The paper hedges explicitly — "This ordering is based on a combination of psychophysical theory and experimental results" and the surrounding text concedes the derivation "will at least convey the process used to devise it." Only two pairs were experimentally tested (position vs. length, position vs. angle); shading/color saturation was never tested in this paper. Likewise the paper labels its assignment of pie charts to the angle task a conjecture: "For this graph we conjecture that the primary elementary visual task ... is perception of angle." Downstream literature contests the applied recommendation, not the paper's contents: Spence & Lewandowsky (1991) found results not supporting pie-chart inferiority for proportion tasks; Kosara & Skau (Judgment Error in Pie Chart Variations) found angle to be the LEAST important cue in pie reading, undercutting C&M's conjectured mechanism; Heer & Bostock (CHI 2010) replicated and largely confirmed the position > length > angle/area ordering. Practically, framed-rectangle charts never achieved adoption and choropleths remain standard newsroom practice — so cite this as the origin of the encoding hierarchy, and do NOT ship "replace choropleths with framed rectangles" as live 2026 guidance without the 40 years of qualification.

### [4] Cleveland & McGill's perceptual ranking of encodings replicates on the web (crowdsourced, N=50/chart, 3,481 trials): position along a common scale is most accurate and significantly beats length, and area/circular-area and color-ish encodings sit at the bottom. BUT the folklore item that angle is worse than length was NOT supported — angle (pie) performed comparably to length in both this study and the 1984 original. Treat 'position > length > angle > area > color' as measured only at its endpoints; the angle-vs-length rung is unsupported.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: http://idl.cs.washington.edu/files/2010-MTurk-CHI.pdf (primary)
Quote: "The ranking of types by accuracy is consistent between the two experiments (Figure 4). Types 1 and 2 are closer in the crowdsourced study; this may be a result of a smaller display mitigating the effect of distance. Types 4 and 5 are more accurate than in the original study, but position encoding still significantly outperformed length encoding. ... Theory also suggests that angle should perform worse than length, but the results do not support this. Cleveland & McGill also did not find angle to perform worse than length, but as stated their position-angle results are not directly comparable to their position-length results."
Verifier evidence (high): Core claim verified verbatim against the primary PDF (Heer & Bostock, CHI 2010), text extracted locally with pdftotext. Method: "Ten charts were constructed at a resolution of 380x380 pixels, for a total of 70 trials (HITs)... For each chart, N=50 subjects were instructed first to identify the smaller of two marked values... only 14 out of 3,481 were incorrect (0.4%)" — confirms N=50/chart and 3,481 trials. Types: T1-T3 position along common scale, T4-T5 length, T6 angle (pie), T7 circular area, T8/T9 rectangular area (Exp 1B). Results, verbatim: "position encoding still significantly outperformed length encoding" and "Theory also suggests that angle should perform worse than length, but the results do not support this. Cleveland & McGill also did not find angle to perform worse than length, but as stated their position-angle results are not directly comparable to their position-length results." Area confirmed at bottom: "psychophysical theory [7,34] predicts area to perform worse than angle, and both to be significantly worse than position... the new results match expectations." Independent corroboration that the angle rung is folklore: Cleveland & McGill's own 1984 ordered list bundles "length, direction, angle" at a SINGLE rank (rank 3) because the tasks could not be separated; the strict length>angle ordering originates with Mackinlay 1986, not with measurement. "The Risks of Ranking" (TVCG 2023, mucollective.northwestern.edu/files/2022-perception-individual-differences.pdf), a Bayesian replication/extension of Cleveland & McGill, concludes canonical rankings "overstate the strength of the evidence" and that between-person variance swamps between-chart differences — supports the claim's caution rather than refuting it. Skau & Kosara 2016 (Arcs, Angles, or Areas) and Kosara 2019 (Evidence for Area as the Primary Visual Cue in Pie Charts) further dissolve the rung by showing pie charts are not read as angle; Zeng & Battle's CHI'23 review states "Cleveland and McGill treated pie charts as primarily angle encodings; however, more recent work suggests that pie charts are perceived more as area encodings." ONE DEFECT REQUIRING CORRECTION BEFORE USE: the sub-clause "and color-ish encodings sit at the bottom" is NOT supported by this source — Heer & Bostock tested no color/hue/saturation encoding; their Experiment 2 is luminance-contrast gridline alpha adjustment, not encoding accuracy. The measured bottom is circular/rectangular area. Likewise "measured only at its endpoints" is loose: the position endpoint is measured, the color endpoint is not measured at all in this paper (that end comes from Cleveland & McGill's theoretical rank 6, shading/color saturation). Weak counter-signal considered and rejected: Zeng & Battle's one-line summary says Heer & Bostock show "bar charts perform better than pie charts," but that review is demonstrably imprecise about this paper (it also miscalls the task a "sort task" when it was proportion estimation) and conflates position with length; the primary text is explicit and overrides it. Source quality is a primary peer-reviewed CHI paper by the authors of the replication, matching the claim's strength; graphical perception is slow-moving and the 2022-2023 follow-ups strengthen rather than date the claim.

### [5] ColorBrewer caps schemes at 12 classes but the authors state only a few schemes stay differentiable at that count; many sequential sets stop at 9 because further subdivision is "perceptually unreliable", and the stated practitioner rule of thumb is that cartographers seldom exceed seven classes on a choropleth — with the exception that isoline maps or maps with very regular spatial patterns can safely exceed seven. This is an attributable (if rule-of-thumb rather than experimentally measured) ceiling on how many colour steps a sequential/diverging encoding can carry.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.cs.rpi.edu/~cutler/classes/visualization/S18/papers/colorbrewer.pdf (primary)
Quote: "These sets have been designed to produce attractive colour schemes of similar appearance for maps ranging from 3 to 12 classes. Not all colour schemes can be expanded to 12 classes, and many of the sequential scheme sets, for example, stop at 9 classes because further divisions within the scheme are perceptually unreliable (Figure 2). This file is the visual vocabulary: **what it looks like**. [`CRAFT.md`](./CRAFT.md)
is the technique arsenal: **how you render it**. They are separate on purpose, and
collapsing them is how runs end up templated.

The distinction is sharp because techniques carry no opinion. `backdrop-filter`
builds the layered translucency of liquid glass, and it also builds the flat frosted
panels of a Swiss layout where the blur is the only softness on the page. A noise
shader is film grain in a cinematic grade and paper tooth in a risograph print. A
spring is playful in a claymorphic world and clinical in a blueprint. The style is
the opinion; the technique is a means of getting there.

The order is fixed. **Style is chosen at Gate B1 with the concept**, from the brief,
the archetype, and the vision. **Techniques are assigned in Loop 2b to serve the
style already chosen.** Reaching for a style because you want to use a shader is the
tail wagging the dog, and it shows in the output. Everything below is a starting
position under `§3`. Read [the guardrails](#the-guardrails) before you pick.

---

## Surface and material

**Glassmorphism.** Translucent panels over a substrate worth seeing through to,
legible from the blur behind them, never from a fill. Depth reads as blur radius,
nearest layer blurring hardest, each panel edged with a 1px light-catching border.
**Implies** `backdrop-filter`, z-layering, `color-mix()` borders. **Fails** as gray
rectangles on a flat background, and breaks `§12` under body copy. **Right when** the
background is itself content.

**Liquid glass.** Apple's 2025 material language, where the panel refracts rather
than merely blurs: content bends passing under the edge, specular highlights track
the light, the shape lenses on scroll. Real implementation is an SDF and shader job;
`backdrop-filter` alone gets glassmorphism with a borrowed name. **Implies** WebGL,
an SDF panel, scroll-linked light, a hard `§13` budget. **Fails** as chrome that
buries the work (`§7`). **Right when** the work is material or hardware.

# Craft

[`STYLES.md`](./STYLES.md) is **what it looks like**. This file is **how you
render it**.

The separation is load-bearing. A style is a destination: a palette, a type
system, a spatial logic, a mood. A technique is the means of arriving: a shader,
a filter, a timeline, a solver. One style is reachable through a dozen
techniques, one technique serves a dozen unrelated styles. Confuse the two and
you get decoration chosen before intent, which is how a run ends up looking like
every other WebGL portfolio.

The order is fixed. The style is chosen at **Gate B1**. Techniques are assigned
**per section** in **Loop 2b (Craft)** to serve that style, each one proven in a
standalone runnable prototype before any section is designed to depend on it.

---

## The mandate

Advanced visual technique is the point. This pipeline exists to produce work
that could not have come out of a template, and the technique layer is where
that becomes visible in the first three seconds.

Pull from whatever best showcases capability. Free rein to look up how to use
any of it: the papers, the shadertoy, the library docs, someone's blog post from
2013. Free rein to pull open-source libraries from a CDN while prototyping.
Everything gets vendored, committed, and self-hosted before ship under `§9`.

**The list below is a starting position, not a boundary.** Nothing here is
required and nothing here is exhaustive. If the right answer for this subject is
a technique with no name yet, build that instead. You have total creative
freedom to design in whatever way best illustrates capability, bounded only by
`§7` (the work is the hero), `§12` (three states) and `§13` (the two tiers).

---

## The arsenal

### Rendering and GPU

The heavy layer. All of it is tier two under `§13`, none of it in the LCP path.

| Technique | What it is | Where it earns its place |
|---|---|---|
| Raymarching + SDFs | Geometry defined as a distance function, marched per pixel | Impossible forms, infinite repetition, soft shadows and ambient occlusion for free. A hero that could not be modeled |
| Domain warping (fbm) | Noise fed into the coordinates of more noise | Organic movement that never loops visibly. Clouds, ink, marble, smoke, atmospheric backgrounds |

input.caveats:
COVERAGE IS THE BIGGEST CAVEAT — this is not the six-area survey that was requested. Of 14 surviving claims, 12 are Area 1 (data/information visualization, and within that mostly perceptual encoding and colour, not charts-in-practice), 2 are Area 2 (modal focus contract, card comparison failure). Area 1 sub-topics with ZERO verified coverage: small multiples, sparklines and micro-charts, dashboard/stat-tile layout, scrollytelling and annotation layers, newsroom conventions (NYT/FT/Pudding/Reuters), table design at density (tabular numerals, decimal alignment, sticky headers), evidence and provenance presentation, screen-reader chart alternatives. Areas 3, 4, 5 and 6 — emerging style movements and AI-default clichés, motion and View Transitions, micro-interactions and timing thresholds, loading/perceived performance — produced NO surviving claims at all and are entirely unaddressed. Do not treat this report as evidence that those areas lack answers; it is evidence that they were not verified in this pass.

SOURCE AGE AND WEIGHT. Two papers (Cleveland & McGill 1984, Harrower & Brewer 2003) carry roughly half the report. Their contents are verbatim-confirmed, but their applied prescriptions are contested downstream: the 'pies fail because of angle' mechanism is empirically overturned (Skau & Kosara 2016, Kosara 2019), framed-rectangle charts never achieved adoption, choropleths remain standard practice, and 'The Risks of Ranking' finds canonical encoding rankings overstate their evidence with between-person variance often exceeding between-encoding differences. Cite the hierarchy as a design prior, never as a law.

THE ONE NN/g CLAIM IS PRACTITIONER-QUALITY, NOT MEASURED. No sample size, no published method, a single-user gaze plot, 2016, and the 'cognitive load' framing is a gloss the article does not support.

VERIFICATION PROCESS LIMITS. Several verifications ran with the session WebSearch budget exhausted (200/200), so contradiction-hunting for the ARIA APG, focus-restore, CSS Color 4 decision-rule and NN/g card claims was done by direct source fetch rather than open search. Those four rest on source inspection alone.

TIME SENSITIVITY. CSS Color 4 is a Candidate Recommendation Draft (17 July 2026), not a REC; the Oklab-default behaviour was empirically confirmed only in Chromium/Edge, with Gecko and WebKit unverified — a portfolio relying on the legacy-vs-non-legacy split should be checked in all three engines. CSS Color 5's color-mix() default sits in tension with the Color 4 legacy carve-out. Everything else here is stable: perceptual findings and the ARIA pattern are not fast-moving.

REFUTED-BUT-PLAUSIBLE. The eleven refuted claims include figures that are probably true in the wider literature (CVD prevalence especially) but failed against the specific sources cited. They need re-sourcing before use, not discarding — and under `§5` (HARD) they cannot ship as-is.
openQuestions: Areas 3-6 are unevidenced and probably cannot be answered with the same source policy: named 2025-26 aesthetic movements, what now reads as AI-default or templated, micro-interaction timing thresholds and skeleton-vs-spinner evidence live in practitioner writing, platform HIG and awards-jury discourse rather than peer review. Does the pipeline accept a lower evidentiary tier for those, with sources flagged as practitioner-grade — or does the anti-template rule get served better by NOT documenting current movements at all, since a documented movement is a movement two runs can converge on?

What are the three states for a chart under §12? FULL / REDUCED / NO-CANVAS is proposed here (final-state still with annotations intact; SVG or semantic table fallback) but nothing in the repo defines it, and the sparkline sizing floor is now genuinely unknown since the ~80px threshold was refuted 0-3. Needs a rendered-and-inspected answer, not a cited one.

Does the pipeline need a provenance mechanism in markup? §5 is HARD and a generated chart is a claim, but STYLES.md and CRAFT.md have nowhere to put a figure's source, date and method. This is the strongest argument for a separate INFORMATION.md, and it is a structural decision, not a content one.

Do Gecko and WebKit implement the CSS Color 4 legacy-sRGB versus Oklab interpolation split identically to Chromium? The opt-in trick (one color(srgb ...) endpoint flips the whole interpolation) is the cheapest quality win in this report and it was verified in one engine only.

input.summary: Only about a quarter of the six-area brief survived adversarial verification: 12 of the 14 confirmed claims sit in Area 1 (data and information visualization — encoding perception, colour-scale construction, interpolation space), 2 sit in Area 2 (modal/drawer focus contract, card-grid failure mode), and Areas 3-6 (emerging style movements, motion and transitions, micro-interactions, perceived performance) produced no surviving claims at all. What the verified evidence does deliver is a defensible spine for the pipeline's missing information-design vocabulary: a perceptual encoding hierarchy (Cleveland & McGill 1984) whose endpoints are measured and whose middle rungs are theory; measured effect sizes including a catastrophic-misreading rate 5.3-7.3x higher for length and angle than for position; a construction grammar for sequential/diverging/qualitative colour with an attributable ~7-class practical ceiling (Brewer); a documented perceptual failure mode for rainbow/jet ramps; and — the single most implementable, zero-byte finding — the normative CSS Color 4 rule that Oklab is the default interpolation space unless legacy sRGB syntax opts you out. On the component side, W3C APG gives a hard two-condition test for when aria-modal is legitimate (inert background AND obscuring visual styling) plus mandatory focus restore, and NN/g documents that card grids defeat comparison tasks because the layout encodes no order. Mapped to the repo, almost none of this belongs in STYLES.md — no verified claim names an aesthetic — it belongs as one new CRAFT.md technique group plus a genuinely new file for chart and container vocabulary, with three flagged tensions against §3 (reinvent every component), §12 and §5.

findings.claim: There is a canonical six-tier perceptual ranking of visual encodings — (1) position on a common scale, (2) position on nonaligned scales, (3) length/direction/angle, (4) area, (5) volume/curvature, (6) shading/colour saturation — but it must be cited as a design PRIOR, not a law: the paper itself calls the ordering 'hypothesized', leaves ties inside tiers 3, 5 and 6 unresolved, and only the position-vs-length and position-vs-angle pairs were ever experimentally tested. The web replication confirms the endpoints (position most accurate, area near the bottom) but does NOT support the folklore rung 'angle is worse than length'.
findings.vote: merged from two claims, each 2-1; both splits were over framing, not over the verbatim source text
findings.evidence: Cleveland & McGill, JASA 79(387):531-554, verbatim: 'The following are the 10 elementary tasks in Figure 1, ordered from most to least accurate: 1. Position along a common scale 2. Positions along nonaligned scales 3. Length, direction, angle 4. Area 5. Volume, curvature 6. Shading, color saturation'; 'Three of the ranks-3, 5, and 6-have more than one task; at the moment there is not enough information to separate the ties'; and the design rule 'Graphs should employ elementary tasks as high in the ordering as possible.' The word 'hypothesize' is the paper's own ('In this section we hypothesize an ordering...'), and tier 2's rank rests on a Weber's-Law argument about framed rectangles, not an experiment. CORRECTION carried from verification: an earlier wording said tiers 1-2-3 were tested; tier 2 was not — only tier 1 vs tier 3 (length, and separately angle) was. Heer & Bostock (CHI 2010, N=50 per chart, 3,481 trials, 0.4% wrong-direction rate) replicate: 'position encoding still significantly outperformed length encoding' and area performs worst, BUT 'Theory also suggests that angle should perform worse than length, but the results do not support this.' The strict length>angle ordering originates with Mackinlay 1986, not with measurement. McColeman et al. ('The Risks of Ranking') find canonical rankings 'overstate the strength of the evidence' and that between-person variance can swamp between-chart differences. NOTE the colour end of the ranking is theoretical in 1984 and was not tested by Heer & Bostock either — their Experiment 2 is gridline luminance-contrast adjustment, not colour encoding accuracy.

findings.claim: The position-over-length-and-angle advantage is measured, not folklore, and the strongest number is about catastrophic misreading rather than average precision: position beat length by factors of 1.4-2.5 and angle by 1.96x, but gross errors (>15.9 percentage points on a 0-100 scale) occurred 5.3x more often for length and 7.3x more often for angle than for position. Encoding choice therefore governs how often a reader is badly wrong, not merely how precise they are.
findings.evidence: Primary source read directly (JSTOR scan; body pages are CCITT images, read visually). Section 4.5 p.544 verbatim: 'In both experiments there were 51 subjects with usable data. ... In the first experiment, position judgments were more accurate than length judgments by factors varying from 1.4 to 2.5. In the second experiment, position judgments were 1.96 times as accurate as angle judgments.' pp.541-542 verbatim: 'Of the 2,550 judgments made by the subjects, 136 had a log error greater than 4. ... the rate of occurrence of large errors for length judgments is 5.3 times that for position judgments. ... 219 of the 4,080 judgments had large errors. Eighty-eight percent ... the rate of occurrence of large errors for the angle judgments is 7.3 times that for the position judgments.' Arithmetic independently reconstructed and self-consistent: 51 subjects x 50 judgments = 2,550; 51 x 80 = 4,080; 3:2 position:length ratio gives 10.4%/1.96% = 5.32; 1:1 position:angle gives 9.45%/1.29% = 7.33. Error metric is log2(|judged% - true%| + 1/8), so 'log error > 4' decodes to >15.9 percentage points. The large-error rate is genuinely ADDITIONAL information because the headline factors use midmeans, chosen 'principally because of the outliers' — the means deliberately trim exactly these tails. Blunders ruled out: 'Only four errors occurred in the choice of which bar or segment was smaller.' SCOPE LIMIT the paper states itself: 'Strictly speaking we cannot do more than assert that the results hold for the particular types of graphs in the experiment' — one task (what percentage one value is of a larger value) on 1984 print stimuli. The >4 threshold is post-hoc with no CI or test statistic reported, so these are descriptive rates, not inferential.

findings.claim: The 1984 applied conclusion is 'replace, don't refine': pie charts, divided bar charts and shaded statistical maps (choropleths) are named as needing 'radical surgery', with dot charts, grouped dot charts and framed-rectangle charts offered as replacements — choropleths condemned because shading/colour saturation sits in the last accuracy tier. Ship the encoding preference, NOT the specific 1984 prescription: framed-rectangle charts never achieved adoption, choropleths remain standard newsroom practice, and the 'pies fail because of angle' mechanism has been empirically overturned.
findings.vote: 3-0 on source contents; the live-2026-guidance qualification is the synthesis's own
findings.evidence: Abstract verbatim: 'The conclusion is that radical surgery on these popular graphs is needed, and as replacements we offer alternative graphical forms-dot charts, dot charts with grouping, and framed-rectangle charts.' Targets named are four, not three: 'bar charts, divided bar charts, pie charts, and statistical maps with shading.' Section 5.3 is titled 'Framed-Rectangle Charts as Replacements for Statistical Maps With Shading'. Bias finding verbatim: 'When the true percentages are in the range of 25-50, subjects tend to underestimate values for these types of judgments' — a systematic under-read in exactly the range most part-of-whole charts live in. QUALIFICATIONS that must travel with any citation: the paper labels its own pie mechanism a conjecture ('we conjecture that the primary elementary visual task ... is perception of angle'); Skau & Kosara (EuroVis/CGF 2016, 35(3):121-130) and Kosara (IEEE VIS 2019, 'Evidence for Area as the Primary Visual Cue in Pie Charts') find angle is the LEAST used cue in pie reading; Spence & Lewandowsky (Applied Cognitive Psychology 1991, 5(1):61-77) found 'little to choose between the pie and bar chart' and pie better for combination/part-of-whole judgments. So: prefer position encodings, and treat part-of-whole and summation tasks as the documented exception rather than banning pies outright.

findings.claim: Colour scales have a construction grammar tied to data type, plus an attributable practical ceiling on step count. Sequential = ordinal/numeric low-to-high, lightness-dominant, 'dark equals more'; diverging = a critical break (mean, median, zero) marked by BOTH hue and lightness change, always multi-hue; qualitative = hue varied with saturation and lightness held near-constant, because arbitrary saturation variation may imply a false order. ColorBrewer caps at 12 classes but most sequential sets stop at 9 because further division is 'perceptually unreliable', and the stated rule of thumb is that cartographers seldom exceed seven classes.
findings.evidence: Harrower & Brewer, The Cartographic Journal 40(1):27-37, 2003, header reads 'REFEREED PAPER'; Brewer authored the ColorBrewer palettes, so this is primary. Verbatim: 'Lightness steps dominate the look of these schemes, usually with light colours for low data values and dark colours for high values. "Dark equals more" is a standard cartographic convention'; 'The break or class in the middle of the sequence is emphasized by a hue and lightness change and should represent a critical value in the data such as the mean, median or zero'; 'Diverging schemes are always multi-hue sequences'; 'Qualitative schemes work best when hue is varied and saturation and lightness are kept or nearly constant. We do not recommend arbitrarily using strong "neon" colours ... and pastel colours ... in the same qualitative colour scheme because these variations in saturation might imply order'; 'many of the sequential scheme sets, for example, stop at 9 classes because further divisions within the scheme are perceptually unreliable'; 'As a general rule of thumb, cartographers seldom use more than seven classes on a choropleth map. Isoline maps, or choropleth maps with very regular spatial patterns, can safely use more than seven data classes.' PRECISION for reuse: 12 is the tool-wide max reached only by qualitative schemes; sequential caps at 9, diverging at 11; the ceiling is about DISCRETE CLASSES, not continuous ramps. KEEP THE HEDGES the source uses: 'might imply order' and 'arbitrarily' — the paper itself ships Paired and Accents as deliberate lightness-varying exceptions, and the seven-class number is explicitly folklore ('rule of thumb') with no citation behind it. TWO ADDITIONS for a portfolio context: Schloss et al. (IEEE TVCG) empirically confirm dark-is-more, but on DARK backgrounds an opaque-is-more bias can invert it — dark-themed portfolio sites should consider light-equals-more; and Okabe-Ito (2008), the standard CVD-safe categorical palette, varies lightness substantially, so accessibility can legitimately require breaking the near-constant-lightness rule.

findings.claim: Rainbow-family colormaps (jet) manufacture false features: a bright mid-range band reads as a local maximum even where the data value is lower, so jet causes magnitude misreading for viewers WITH AND WITHOUT colour-vision deficiency. This is a documented perceptual effect with a mechanically verifiable cause, not a style preference — though post-2023 the field's position is that the induced categorization is task-dependent, not universally harmful.
findings.evidence: Nunez, Anderton & Renslow, PLOS ONE 13(7):e0199239, verbatim: 'An example of how the data may be misinterpreted are evident in the bright yellow spots in (b) and (c), which appear to represent significantly higher values than the surrounding regions. However, in fact, the dark red (in b) and dark yellow (in c) actually represent the highest values.' The obvious refutation — that both panels are CVD simulations — fails on the figure caption: '(a) perceptually uniform grayscale, (b) jet, (c) jet as it appears to someone with red-green colorblindness, and (d) viridis', so panel (b) is jet at NORMAL colour vision. MECHANISM INDEPENDENTLY COMPUTED during verification: WCAG sRGB relative luminance across jet gives L=0.0455 at the data maximum (x=1.00, dark red) versus a peak L=0.9184 at x=0.62 (bright yellow) — the mid-range band is 20.2x brighter than the true maximum, with two interior luminance local maxima (x=0.38 cyan, x=0.62 yellow). This is a reproducible property of the ramp's construction, viewer-independent. Corroborated by Borland & Taylor, IEEE CG&A 2007 'Rainbow Color Map (Still) Considered Harmful'; Crameri et al., Nature Communications 2020; Stoelzle & Stein, HESS 25:4549 (2021). The leading rainbow-DEFENCE paper (Ware, Turton, Bujack et al., IEEE TVCG 2023) confirms the mechanism rather than disputing it — rainbow schemes 'induce categorization', aiding global/distributional reading while suppressing local detail — so write it as 'documented perceptual effect causing magnitude misreading' rather than blanket condemnation. Practical rule unchanged for this pipeline: use perceptually-uniform OKLCH-derived or viridis-class ramps.

findings.claim: CSS Color 4 normatively makes Oklab the DEFAULT interpolation space for gradients, transitions, animations, filters, color-mix() and relative colour syntax — but with a legacy carve-out: hex, named, rgb(), hsl() and hwb() colours still interpolate in gamma-encoded sRGB. Authors opt in to perceptually even ramps by writing at least one endpoint as color(srgb r g b) or by naming the interpolation space. The spec also gives a four-case decision rule for which space fits which job, and names sRGB's failure mode as 'overly dark or greyish mixes'. This is the highest-value finding for the pipeline: zero bytes, no runtime, pure syntax discipline.
findings.evidence: W3C CR Draft 17 July 2026, section 13.1 'Color Space for Interpolation', normative prose (not a Note), verbatim: 'If the host syntax does not define what color space interpolation should take place in, it defaults to Oklab.' / 'However, user agents must handle interpolation between legacy sRGB color formats (hex colors, named colors, rgb(), hsl() or hwb() ...) in gamma-encoded sRGB space.' / 'authors can choose to opt-in to better interpolation, even between sRGB colors, by using the non-legacy color(srgb r g b) form for at least one of their colors, or by explicitly specifying an interpolation color space.' Host syntax is enumerated by the spec as '<gradient>, filter, animation, transition, color-mix(), relative color syntax'. EMPIRICALLY CONFIRMED in headless Chrome stable (macOS), Web Animations midpoint at currentTime=500/1000 linear: '#ff0000'->'#0000ff' = rgb(128, 0, 128) (gamma sRGB); 'color(srgb 1 0 0)'->'color(srgb 0 0 1)' = oklab(0.539974 0.0962087 -0.0928316); MIXED '#ff0000'->'color(srgb 0 0 1)' = the same oklab value — one non-legacy endpoint flips the whole interpolation. wpt.fyi css-color-4-colors-default-to-oklab-gradient.html and legacy-color-gradient.html both pass on Chromium stable. Four-case decision rule, verbatim: linear-light (CIE XYZ, srgb-linear, display-p3-linear) 'because they are linear in light intensity' for physical light mixing; Oklab/Lab when 'colors need to be evenly spaced perceptually (such as in a gradient)'; OkLCh/LCH 'If avoiding graying out in color mixing is desired, i.e. maximizing chroma throughout the transition'; sRGB for legacy compatibility 'even though it produces poorer results (overly dark or greyish mixes)'. Oklab provenance, section 9.2 (labelled non-normative): 'produced by numerical optimization of a large dataset of visually similar colors, and has improved hue linearity, hue uniformity, and chroma uniformity compared to CIE LCH' — corroborated by Ottosson's derivation and by Raph Levien's independent critique, whose only objection is the cube-root transfer function's near-black behaviour, not hue or chroma uniformity. CAVEATS: the four-case guidance is advisory ('may be more appropriate', 'work well for'), not a MUST; CSS Color 5 states 'If no color interpolation method is specified, assume Oklab' for color-mix() with the example color-mix(firebrick, goldenrod) == color-mix(in oklab, ...), in tension with the Color 4 legacy carve-out; behaviour verified only in Chromium/Edge — Gecko and WebKit unverified; the document is a Candidate Recommendation Draft, not a REC.

findings.claim: Modal drawers, sheets and side panels have a hard, citable accessibility contract with two parts. (1) aria-modal="true" is legitimate ONLY when both application code prevents all users from interacting with outside content AND visual styling obscures it — a panel that only dims the background, or only sets aria-modal without inerting, violates the pattern and actively harms AT users. (2) On close, focus returns to the invoking element, unless that element no longer exists or the workflow dictates another target.
findings.evidence: W3C WAI ARIA APG, verbatim rationale and rule: 'Because marking a dialog modal by setting aria-modal to true can prevent users of some assistive technologies from perceiving content outside the dialog, users of those technologies will experience severe negative ramifications if a dialog is marked modal but does not behave as a modal for other users' — 'So, mark a dialog modal only when both: 1. Application code prevents all users from interacting in any way with content outside of it. 2. Visual styling obscures the content outside of it.' Focus restore, verbatim: 'When a dialog closes, focus returns to the element that invoked the dialog unless either: The invoking element no longer exists. Then, focus is set on another element that provides logical work flow' — with a worked example (toolbar 'Add Rows' -> focus lands in the first cell of the first new row). NORMATIVE CORROBORATION stronger than APG: WHATWG HTML 'close the dialog' algorithm step 12 runs the focusing steps for the previously focused element, captured at 'show a modal dialog' step 16 — so for native <dialog> + showModal() the BROWSER does the restore and it is not author work; it is an author deliverable only for custom div-built drawers, sheets and bottom sheets, which is exactly what this pipeline generates. MDN independently: 'When a modal element is displayed, authors should mark all other contents as inert' and 'ARIA doesn't change anything about an element's function or behavior ... The features that make the element actually modal must be implemented by the developer.' PRECISION: APG is non-normative authoring guidance using descriptive wording ('focus returns'), not 'must' — the imperative strength comes from WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A) and the HTML spec, and should be attributed there. 'Drawer' is this report's extension; it holds only for drawers that are genuinely modal — a non-modal side panel is a different pattern with weaker obligations. NOTE the separate cyclic focus-trap claim (Tab wraps last->first, Shift+Tab first->last) was REFUTED 0-3 as stated and must not be shipped as a normative W3C requirement without re-verification.

findings.claim: Card grids have a documented failure mode for comparison tasks: because a flexible card layout encodes no order and places attributes unpredictably from item to item, eyetracking shows users scanning back and forth in a semirandom pattern and re-visiting the same items — measurably harder than a vertical list where each attribute sits in a predictable position. Directly relevant to the pipeline's default 'grid of project cards' output.
findings.vote: 2-1; in-house unpublished eyetracking, single-user gaze plot, 2016
findings.evidence: NN/g (Page Laubheimer, 2016-11-06), verbatim and stronger than the originally cited line: 'Cards are also a poor choice when users need to compare between multiple options, since cards often aren't structured in a predictable way from item to item; our eyetracking research revealed that users look back and forth multiple times between items when they compare them.' Also 'The flexible-card layout does not clearly indicate a hierarchy of stories in order, so the user looks around back and forth in a semirandom pattern, looking for any compelling information'; 'Card layouts typically deemphasize the ranking of content'; and the contrast case 'A vertical list easily supports scanning for price from one product to the next, as this information is placed in a predictable location on each item in the list ... The irregular layout makes this comparison behavior a more difficult undertaking than a vertical list.' WEAKNESSES to flag when citing: 'raising cognitive load' is a gloss — the article never says cognitive load, interaction cost or effort; its actual words are 'a more difficult undertaking than a vertical list', and the finding should be written as slower/harder scanning. The eyetracking is unpublished in-house work: no N, no method, and the illustrated gaze plot is a single user. Treat as credible qualitative practitioner evidence, not a quantified effect. Note also that the adjacent, stronger claim — that NN/g explicitly recommends a vertical list INSTEAD of cards for homogeneous collections such as a portfolio of similar projects — was REFUTED 0-3 and must not be attributed to this article.

findings.claim: Several widely-repeated numbers commonly used to justify chart and component decisions did NOT survive verification against their cited sources and must not be shipped as attributed fact. Notably: the CVD prevalence figures (8% of men / 0.5% of women), 'viridis is not CVD-safe, cividis is', the >7% rainbow-distortion figure, the sparkline sizing floor (~80px height, 40px too small), the 8px minimum gridline spacing, the 1:1-aspect-ratio treemap penalty, the ColorBrewer 'scheme type determines CVD safety' rule, and the cyclic focus-trap-as-normative-W3C-requirement.
findings.vote: refuted 0-3 or 1-2; absence of verification, not proof of falsity
findings.evidence: Eleven claims were put to three-vote adversarial verification and failed to reach consensus against the source URLs they were attributed to. This matters operationally because section 5 of PRINCIPLES.md is a HARD rule ('Every claim traces to evidence ... No source, no quote'), so any of these numbers appearing in a generated site's copy, chart annotation or design rationale would be an unsourced claim by the pipeline's own standard. IMPORTANT EPISTEMIC NOTE: refutation here means the verifiers could not confirm the number in the cited source at the cited strength — several of these (CVD prevalence in particular) are likely true in the wider literature but need a different, correctly-attributed primary source before use. The design consequences that DO survive without these numbers: redundant non-colour encoding is required by section 12 and WCAG regardless of prevalence statistics; sequential ramps should be verified by desaturating the rendered chart rather than by citing a lightness-monotonicity theorem; and sparkline/gridline minimum sizes are currently UNKNOWN to this pipeline and should be set by rendering and looking, not by a cited threshold.

findings.claim: MAPPING TO REPO — the verified evidence maps almost entirely to CRAFT.md and to a new file, NOT to STYLES.md, because not one surviving claim describes an aesthetic. Recommend: (a) one new CRAFT.md group 'Information design' with rows in the existing three-column shape; (b) a new file (suggest INFORMATION.md, referenced from both) holding the chart-selection and component-container vocabulary, since it is neither a look nor a rendering technique; (c) no new STYLES.md entries from this evidence — writing them would mean inventing mechanics the sources do not supply.
findings.vote: synthesis inference from the verified findings plus direct reading of the repo files
findings.evidence: CRAFT.md rows are | Technique | What it is | Where it earns its place |. Proposed rows, all CSS/SVG-native, all shell-tier (<100KB, no runtime, section-13-safe): 'Position-first encoding' / 'Metric values mapped to position on a common scale rather than angle or area' / 'Cleveland & McGill: position beats angle by 1.96x and produces 7.3x fewer gross misreads. Any stat block, result table or before/after figure'. 'OKLCH interpolation' / 'At least one gradient or transition endpoint written as color(srgb ...) or oklch(), or an explicit in-oklch' / 'Zero bytes, no JS: turns every gradient and hover transition perceptually even and kills sRGB greying, per CSS Color 4 section 13.1'. 'Perceptually-uniform ramp' / 'Sequential and diverging scales built in OKLCH with monotonic lightness, capped at ~7 discrete steps' / 'Survives greyscale and CVD by construction; testable by desaturating the render'. 'Diverging break' / 'Hue AND lightness change at a meaningful zero or mean' / 'Any signed metric — growth, delta, sentiment — where the break is the story'. 'Inert modal contract' / 'aria-modal only with real inerting plus obscuring styling; focus restored to the invoker on close' / 'The two APG conditions, non-negotiable under section 12; native <dialog>+showModal() gets restore free, custom drawers do not'. 'Index over grid' / 'A vertical, consistently-positioned list or editorial index instead of a card grid when items are compared' / 'NN/g eyetracking: card layouts encode no order, producing semirandom scanning; also cheaper and better for section 7'. STYLES.md entries take the shape **Name.** mechanics **Implies** X **Fails** Y **Right when** Z — none of the 14 claims supplies a mechanics sentence, a failure mode and a right-when for a LOOK, so writing STYLES entries from this evidence would be fabrication. The new-material case: chart selection and container patterns are neither 'what it looks like' nor 'how you render it', and forcing them into either file collapses the distinction that the opening paragraph of STYLES.md calls load-bearing.

Nothing is a template' is in direct tension with a fixed chart and container vocabulary; the resolution is to state the encoding hierarchy as a CONSTRAINT on invention, not a component library. (2) The reduced-motion and no-WebGL triple-state rule under section 12 is written for animation and shaders and has no defined answer for a chart. (3) Section 5 (HARD) plus the refuted-claims finding means any chart the pipeline generates carries a provenance obligation the repo has no machinery for.

findings.evidence: Section 3 reads 'Reinvent every component, every run. Nothing is a template.' A shipped chart vocabulary is exactly the templating this forbids — so entries must be phrased as invariants (encode with position where the value must be read accurately; give a diverging scale a meaningful break) that leave the FORM free, mirroring how CRAFT.md already frames its arsenal as 'a starting position, not a boundary'. Section 12 requires 'a still frame someone art-directed, not animation: none' and 'a no-WebGL fallback' — for a chart the three states are undefined and should be specified: FULL = animated entrance or transition; REDUCED = the chart drawn at its final state with the annotation layer intact, never a blank axis; NO-CANVAS = inline SVG or a semantic <table>, since SVG charts are already shell-tier and canvas is only needed above a few thousand marks. Section 13 is satisfied by every technique proposed — SVG charts, OKLCH colour and list-over-grid layouts are all HTML/CSS/SVG, add no runtime, and keep the LCP path clear; nothing here needs a charting library, and pulling one would violate section 9 (own every asset) unless vendored. Section 5 is HARD and its text is 'No source, no quote' — a generated chart is a claim, so the pipeline needs a place to put figure provenance (source, date, method) in the markup, which neither STYLES.md nor CRAFT.md provides; this is the strongest structural argument for a separate INFORMATION.md rather than bolted-on rows.

input.caveats:
COVERAGE IS THE BIGGEST CAVEAT — this is not the six-area survey that was requested. Of 14 surviving claims, 12 are Area 1 (data and information visualization, and within that mostly perceptual encoding and colour, not charts-in-practice), 2 are Area 2 (modal focus contract, card comparison failure). Area 1 sub-topics with ZERO verified coverage: small multiples, sparklines and micro-charts, dashboard and stat-tile layout, scrollytelling and annotation layers, newsroom conventions (NYT/FT/Pudding/Reuters), table design at density (tabular numerals, decimal alignment, sticky headers), evidence and provenance presentation, screen-reader chart alternatives. Areas 3, 4, 5 and 6 — emerging style movements and AI-default cliches, motion and View Transitions, micro-interactions and timing thresholds, loading and perceived performance — produced NO surviving claims at all and are entirely unaddressed. Do not read this as evidence that those areas lack answers; it is evidence that they were not verified in this pass.

SOURCE AGE AND WEIGHT. Two papers (Cleveland & McGill 1984, Harrower & Brewer 2003) carry roughly half the report. Their contents are verbatim-confirmed, but their applied prescriptions are contested downstream: the 'pies fail because of angle' mechanism is empirically overturned (Skau & Kosara 2016, Kosara 2019), framed-rectangle charts never achieved adoption, choropleths remain standard practice, and 'The Risks of Ranking' finds canonical encoding rankings overstate their evidence with between-person variance often exceeding between-encoding differences. Cite the hierarchy as a design prior, never as a law.

THE ONE NN/g CLAIM IS PRACTITIONER-QUALITY, NOT MEASURED. No sample size, no published method, a single-user gaze plot, 2016, and the 'cognitive load' framing is a gloss the article does not support.

VERIFICATION PROCESS LIMITS. Several verifications ran with the session WebSearch budget exhausted (200/200), so contradiction-hunting for the ARIA APG, focus-restore, CSS Color 4 decision-rule and NN/g card claims was done by direct source fetch rather than open search. Those four rest on source inspection alone.

TIME SENSITIVITY. CSS Color 4 is a Candidate Recommendation Draft (17 July 2026), not a REC; the Oklab-default behaviour was empirically confirmed only in Chromium and Edge, with Gecko and WebKit unverified — a portfolio relying on the legacy-versus-non-legacy split should be checked in all three engines. CSS Color 5's color-mix() default sits in tension with the Color 4 legacy carve-out. Everything else here is stable: perceptual findings and the ARIA pattern are not fast-moving.

REFUTED-BUT-PLAUSIBLE. The eleven refuted claims include figures that are probably true in the wider literature (CVD prevalence especially) but failed against the specific sources cited. They need re-sourcing before use, not discarding — and under section 5 (HARD) they cannot ship as-is.
openQuestions: Areas 3-6 are unevidenced and probably cannot be answered under the same source policy: named 2025-26 aesthetic movements, what now reads as AI-default or templated, micro-interaction timing thresholds and skeleton-versus-spinner evidence live in practitioner writing, platform HIG and awards-jury discourse rather than peer review. Does the pipeline accept a lower evidentiary tier for those, with sources flagged as practitioner-grade — or does the anti-template rule get served better by NOT documenting current movements at all, since a documented movement is one that two runs can converge on?

What are the three states for a chart under section 12? FULL / REDUCED / NO-CANVAS is proposed here (final-state still with annotations intact; SVG or semantic table fallback) but nothing in the repo defines it, and the sparkline sizing floor is now genuinely unknown since the ~80px threshold was refuted 0-3. Needs a rendered-and-inspected answer, not a cited one.

Does the pipeline need a provenance mechanism in markup? Section 5 is HARD and a generated chart is a claim, but STYLES.md and CRAFT.md have nowhere to put a figure's source, date and method. This is a structural decision, not a content one, and it is the strongest argument for a separate INFORMATION.md.

Do Gecko and WebKit implement the CSS Color 4 legacy-sRGB versus Oklab interpolation split identically to Chromium? The opt-in trick — one color(srgb ...) endpoint flips the whole interpolation — is the cheapest quality win in this report and it was verified in one engine only.
